A Note for my Sister

Roderick Tenderson - 1932.

I have made much progress in my research over these last months. My host has furnished me with appropriate accommodations and the food is hearty with a warmth that lifts the spirits. While I am gracious for their hospitality, I have yet to give my appreciation in person. The caretaker assures me that they are on extended holiday, but their absence is peculiar. Something about this arrangement unnerves me, though I cannot for the life of me determine its source.

It is but a minor xenophobia, a fear of the unknown that sets my eyes to dwelling on the dark corners of this unfamiliar, decaying, but immaculate estate. At night, I perceive to hear the echoes of a distant hammering, the scraping of metal on metal, the rumble of thunder. Yet when I sash my nightgown tight and emerge upon the veranda, the misty countryside is spread wide under the moon and I am greeted with nothing but the echo of cicadas and the smell of tulips in the night air.

The business at hand: Included within the accompanying package is an extensive collection of clippings, journal entries, and letters chronicling the storied history of this peculiar estate and its proprietors. Their contents are fascinating and I have arranged them in a semblance of order which tells a vivid, extraordinary tale.

I expect to return to London shortly, but I have posted this ahead of my arrival so as to make the burden lighter for me. I fear I don't have the same fortitude that I once did. If perchance something were to happen to me, I trust you will ensure its publication in whatever form you see fit.

As always, I think of you fondly. Give mother my warmest regards.

Roderick

Letter from {{0=...|Oliver|James|Olivia|...}} - 14 July, 1831.

It is with great reticence that I relay a grievous event which occurred upon my arrival. It is my hope that in penning these thoughts my mind will find solace from the foul images that have so firmly embedded themselves.

I will spare you the details of the journey to that dismal village to settle my deceased father's affairs. But upon entering its unpaved limits, my spouse drew my attention to several men and women galloping towards the town center, where there was a loud commotion and gathering of individuals. Intrigued by the local pageantry, I resolved to indulge my curiosity. I rapped my knuckles against the roof of the carriage and asked for the driver to turn towards the festivities.

He did not respond to my insistence. Nor did he respond when I thrice repeated my command. Frustrated, I angled my head out of the carriage window in order to speak more firmly. That is when I spied the horrific source of his obstinate and wise decision. For the briefest of moments — though a moment long enough for it to be etched within my memory forever — I saw the source of the commotion: A crowd of people surrounded a tall wooden stage where, swinging slowly from a thick hemp noose, hung a youthful woman. Her lifeless eyes stared in my direction before her form was obscured by buildings.

An irrational fear has gripped the populace. I swear it. The region is rife with superstitious traditions - traditions that do not mix well with the Church's rigid moral compass. When an individual from this close-knit community emerges from shuttered windows, they eye me as one would a foreigner, with sideways glances that make each excursion there insufferable. Accusations of witchcraft and voodooism erupt with increasing fervor, and paranoia weaves its tendrils into their minds.

Maybe this forced solitude will prove beneficial to my wits, as even amidst this clamor I find myself unnaturally focused. I have recently discovered my father's leather-bound journal and, while somewhat trite, I feel it has sparked something within me - a direction for my future studies, perhaps. Maybe it will offer some amusement in these trying times.
Shared Mania

{{0=...|Oliver|James|Olivia|...}}'s Journal - 16 September, 1850. Romania.

It is nearing midnight now, and I struggle to find my words. Is this remorse I feel, or elation? Even as I was swept into the midst of the frightened crowd, watching the flames swirl upwards, I was spellbound by their savagery. I could not imagine that this paranoia would be exercised so bluntly!

It began over supper with my siblings: The Blacksmith - accused of practicing witchcraft - was carried past our brasserie to the steps of Town Hall. He wailed and protested his innocence, and when allowed use of his hands, he immediately accused Henriette, the town Butcher, of beguiling him. Within moments, he dramatically convulsed and acted as if under a trance when she decried his accusation.

As we investigated the commotion that had interrupted our dessert course more closely, the Blacksmith's eyes blazed with fiery determination. He pled with us specifically. He would offer us his services, whatever we needed to spare his life.

The Butcher was pressed to the steps of Town Hall. Silent, innocent as she approached, and forlorn. We knew that Henriette would offer the same deal.

There was no way to slake the public's thirst for catharsis without bloodshed. Tonight, a witch was burned.

Journal of {{0=...|Oliver|James|Olivia|...}} - {{1=...|14 July, 1863|...}}

My lust for fame knows no boundaries. Whether fulfilled through ethical means or the mark of infamy, I was born with a yearning to be known both far and wide for my scientific exploits. These narcissistic thoughts plague my waking hours and infect my dreams!
My thirst for knowledge is unquenchable. Each evening I search through ancient tomes and scholarly texts, scouring every printed word and mathematical formula as if it were the last I will ever read.

I have spent days upon days locked away within my secret laboratory. It is as though my entire existence is singularly focused on the pursuit of scientific excellence. I do not care if it drives me mad! If my contributions can advance Science even by a minute amount it will all be worth it!

I am surrounded by simple-minded human filth. How dare they look at such an affluent individual with judgement in their eyes? How dare they interfere with an aristocrat's greatest, most valuable work? Oh, they will PAY for their insolence!

I will not suffer fools. It is just as important for a peasant or a king to know their place in the presence of my genius. I will show them all how to pay homage to their betters. Soon there will be no way to ignore my inspirational presence and I will command respect!

I find pleasure in the simple act of experimentation. Every tested hypothesis is a delectable morsel to be savored. And is it not my obligation - my right - to share this sense of wonder with the world? The wretches deserve to be entertained - for what is life without spectacle and indulgence?

I hope you will forgive the direct manner in which this letter is received. Due to recent events, I no longer entrust my correspondence to postal carriers and prefer to hire discrete private couriers. This message is meant for your eyes only and I will not allow those who so blatantly scheme against me an opportunity to uncover my motives!

This town has gone mad.

I have only just been situated these past few months with my spouse and close servants, and scarcely familiarized myself with the thatched-roofs and bucolic scenery, yet already I have seen the fires blaze at night, the screams of the damned, and the gibbet creaking under the weight of swinging bodies. The mob comes with torches in the evening and rips the accused from their residences. It appears that my parent's warnings proved true. The occult hysteria that they endured has returned in earnest! I fear that I may be next!

Even my own cousins have begun to eye me like mongrel dogs, yearning for scraps. In their jealous mania, they wish to uncover my secrets and claim them for their own. I can see how they desire to place the blame upon me - to distract me from completing my family's important scientific work! It would break my heart to see ill come to them, yet if they continue in their provocations, I will not hesitate to unleash the fires of hell upon them.

But I am secure in my ambitions. I have uncovered my true purpose. I will not succumb to fear. My secret work consumes my waking hours and I will stop at nothing to see it come to fruition!

Correspondence - {{0=...|Oliver|James|Olivia|...}} - 25 June, 1926

It feels like ages since I have written. The village that we once sojourned to all those years ago has fallen silent. It's crumbling defenses are a reminder - a metaphor for the crippling isolation of xenophobia. Even now I remember those accursed city walls that sapped my youthful vitality with every visit into the murky depths of that place - a place that could never be rebuilt after the hideous Experiment was unleashed.

Yet, even now the indomitable pull of my family's infamous work tears at my very soul! No. I cannot carry on a legacy of fear that left an entire town and estate in ruins. My colleagues at the university have no reverence for me. They laugh so heartily when I tell them the town in which I was birthed. I do not blame them. My hope is that I shall never see that foul place again. How could my family cultivate such an embarrassing line of thinking?

As I pen this note, my lawyer has made arrangements for a transfer of ownership - the deed to that wretched estate will soon finally be wrested from my hands and with it, the insidious efforts contained within will be buried forever.

Journal Entry: {{0=...|Oliver|James|Olivia|...}} - 1 March, 1924.

I see now how wrong I had been. True inspiration, true science, true art, it emerges from isolation. Isolation is the catalyst. With silence and contemplation, the ability to truly focus without distractions, this is where perfection and enlightenment is achieved.

The citizens of {{1=...|Town|...}} were right in their decision. Outside influences only pollute the mind and distract.

One must be self-reliant and self-motivated. Science is instinctual. Brilliance doesn't come from universities. No one was ever remembered as the world's greatest team player. No.

The rest of the world may be unaware of my family's work, but that is all part of my ingenious plan. Today, I retreat to my laboratory. Soon, I will emerge from my scientific cocoon more brilliant than ever before and the world will tremble at my feet!

Correspondence from {{0=...|Oliver|James|Olivia|...}} - 14 June, 1925

If you can smell the scent of tea and rich pastries on this paper before you, it is because I write this letter to you from one of my favorite shops along the main street. The shuffling footsteps and metal din of automobiles along concrete allows my thoughts to wander. I find it disagreeably bright in these parts nowadays, but at least they serve a damn fine cuppa. There are definite benefits to traveling merchants offering a steady supply of fine goods.

It appears we have emerged from the dismal environs of yesteryear into a full springtime bloom. My family may have made a few missteps, but it seems their kind-hearted souls (of which I was not aware) won the day and assuaged the fears of the populace. I will say that it is rather enjoyable to sketch out new scientific diagrams in broad daylight without scrutiny.

There are even some willing to volunteer their time towards my "eccentric hobbies" as they call them. Such insufferable fools. I will take pleasure in exploiting their ignorance. But, I will try to be sensible about it - it is unseasonable weather for painful howling.

Anyway, send my best wishes to your mother and do not tarry too long.

Yours Always,

Letter from {{0=...|Oliver|James|Olivia|...}} - 4 January, 1924

It finally happened. They destroyed it all. Mobs with actual torches and pitchforks, I tell you, knocked down my properly erected fencing and stormed the estate, destroying my parents' work. The curs had the audacity to arrive unannounced - had I not heard the hounds eviscerating several members of the crowd, I may not have escaped before being swallowed up by the flames.

The grounds still remain fallow and singed by ash, enveloping the plot in a vast, dreary grayness. My entreaties to the governor have been met with indifference and ridicule. It is clear that I will receive no financial remuneration for this riotous behavior. Am I to be forever punished for the sins of my father?

No matter! What do they know of loss? I have lost everything. My family's legacy is in tatters. They drive us away as if we are the outsiders, like foreign beggars.

This is not over. I will have vengeance. This paltry village will rue the day it crossed, {{0=...|Oliver|James|Olivia|...}}, the Fourth!

Also, if you would be so kind as to furnish me a small loan, it would certainly expedite my ability to obtain said revenge.

Journal Entry - {{0=...|Oliver|James|Olivia|...}} - 16 August, 1929

Sunday: I had the glorious dream again - it never fails to reinvigorate me, as I could relive that moment each night for the remainder of my years and be content.

I watch with steady eyes as my family's creation, {{3=...|Iron Maiden|...}}, with cathartic ambivalence, lifts the severed head of {{2=...|The Butcher|...}} high into the air. I feel the searing heat of burning oil, hear the hiss of rising steam and smoke, and smell the rusted iron in the air. The crowded arena cheered even as their leader was torn from his makeshift throne and tossed lifeless to the dusty Earth, blood pooling beneath, dark and thick as motor oil.

These images appear in my mind like light on silver even as my weathered hands strain to grasp the quill. My last act of defiance, perhaps. But what is the worth of toppling a regional tyrant? All this effort to shake the world, and barely one square kilometer has been rattled.

The inmates have moved on. The town is an empty, ruined field without vegetation - a decaying pile of ash, rust, and mud. Some days my mind feels the same. The sense of peace does nothing to stem this emptiness of purpose inside of me.{{5=?| An old man visits now and then - a friend of the family with a withered face that he keeps wrapped tightly with a scarf.}}

What a waste contentment is! What a terrible investment! I only hope my progeny will leave this broken land behind and forge a new path.

Letter from {{0=...|Oliver|James|Olivia|...}} - 5 May, 1925

The customs of Transylvania are even stranger than I remember. I had vague recollections from my youth of being schooled in our home and shielded from the smoky village residing deep in that valley, but I could not have guessed the true reasoning behind it all.

I have forged an alliance with the local government based on my parent's good will. They have democratically elected {{2=...|The Butcher|...}} and have even offered to provide materials and assistance for my continued experimentations. I would understand your initial apprehension at the moniker of {{2=...|The Butcher|...}}, but I assure you that the title is derived from a regional dialect and is part of tradition. They have even fashioned a gaming arena of sorts within the town proper, where a particularly aggressive form of sparring is practiced.

In fact, I find this region to be surprisingly inclusive and accepting of the avant-garde, which suits my needs as you might expect. I have even scheduled a meeting this weekend with a local Count. He claims to have been a friend of the family and has resumed interest in business ventures within the district.

It is my hope that this letter finds you well. The news I hear from Bucharest is positive, with a seasonable chill in the air and continued peace. As such, I pray you will indulge me in forgoing pleasantries and moving to matters of business with haste.

The institution in {{1=...|Town|...}} has been an unrivaled success. A steady stream of those suffering from insanities and delusions have been shipped here from other parts of the country. Yet still officials always wonder how we run such an efficient operation even as funding remains remarkably low. Which is why I must repeat my strong request from my previous letter: we require more fresh patients to treat. Our near one hundred percent release rate has left several vacancies in the facility and we are in dire need to obtain more.

How do you know we haven't simply been failing to treat them and then disposing of their bodies? Why are there bloodstains on the envelope of my previous letter? These are all important questions.

But, I ask you now - why question results?

Letter from {{0=...|Oliver|James|Olivia|...}} - 30 March, 1892. Romania.

I tell you, these damn peasants actually built a wall around their own town. In the 1800's no less! These fools have traded paranoia for utter delusion!

Do they expect a foreign government to set up a military line and trebuchets to lay siege to this backwater stronghold? What on earth would it offer them? Trade has suffered. Prices have risen. And most importantly, with the caravans left to go elsewhere, I must find alternative ways to procure knowledge.

Why just this week, I was enraged by the audacity of the intrusion into my affairs! I, the rightful heir to a considerable estate, was forced to suffer the indignity of a physical inspection at what appeared to be a freshly fashioned gateway to the village where I was born. And then, to infer that I was bound by duty to prove my citizenship? My spouse was so manhandled that they were forced to spend the next week in their bedroom consumed by anxious thoughts.

Curse this infernal world filled with frustrations and complications at every turn! If only these regressive tendencies toward isolationism could have been resolved in another way! Surely, you can determine how dire the situation has become if it has rattled my notoriously pragmatic disposition. How can one change the world when it so decidedly wants to remain the same?

Mark my words, I would sooner watch these ramparts crumble than allow them to destroy my spirit. I will find a way to circumvent this oppressive state and preserve my legacy at all costs!
Minor Recompense

Letter from {{0=...|Oliver|James|Olivia|...}} - 9 February, 1892. Romania.

I apologize for the tardiness of my reply, but settling the matters of my inheritance has uncovered distressing revelations that haunt my waking hours. It is terrible. And by terrible, I mean decent, cheerful, and painfully dull. People stroll around this inviting town, greet each other with smiles, and share baked goods. Baked goods! How are they so blind to the dark realities of the world? How did we arrive at such an excruciatingly positive conclusion?

While other institutions across Europe experienced the ravenous strain of overcrowding, our town’s well-funded lunatic asylum proved a luminous model of rehabilitation. Restraints were traded for personal care from the staff and a work release program was expanded for patients eager to assimilate themselves into society once again, with the skills to succeed.

It is an interesting concept in theory, but one which we know will only end in folly. When I made a brief visit to the Asylum Program (as they now so boldly call it), they even attempted to evaluate me as if I had been admitted. Apparently, the country has turned to more civilized ways to disenfranchise individuals that they fear — not to mention the additional taxes levied against legitimate entrepreneurs such as myself.

Like mighty Atlas, I will accept these heavy charges. While I disagree with their methodology, and the expenses of this progressive approach will certainly be a financial burden, access to skilled labor does appeal to me from an efficiency standpoint, if they have the stomach for it.

The days are certainly bright here in the valley, but in the end, this light will only make my family's work shine more brilliantly!
Understanding and Support

Journal of {{0=...|Oliver|James|Olivia|...}} - (Cont.)

Whether for love or purpose - I know not which drove my decision - I broke into the mausoleum housing my spouse and applied the solution to their skeletal features. Following the exact recipe for the formulae proved difficult, but I was able to make due with local alternatives.

With a billow of emerald smoke, I saw the features of my long-dead spouse reform into the perfect form I remembered from my youth. I had done it!

I could scarcely trust my own senses. It worked? And without any defects visible or otherwise?

I embraced them, and though they were startled by the decades' difference in our ages, they returned the embrace. I am a genius!

However, I find that their temperament is uneven. On one particular evening, they suddenly burst open the doors of our carriage and fled into an alleyway before I could recover my senses enough to make chase.

I observed in abject horror as their neck spun unnaturally around to face me while their body remained stationary. Their feral lips were covered in blood and the fresh body of some unfortunate man lay eviscerated on the cobblestones, their insides glistening in the haze of a crescent moon.

Generally though, they are back to their normal selves.
